title: A burning groundnut and a food label: what the numbers say about your food

summary.text: Hold a groundnut in a flame and it keeps burning on its own for about a minute. Yet the school chart calls groundnuts a body-building food, not an energy food. Your child burns a groundnut, a cashew and a piece of dry coconut under a tumbler of water, measures the heat with a thermometer, and works out how much heat was lost. They cook rice and find that 100 grams of cooked rice holds only about a third of the energy in 100 grams of raw rice. They learn to read a food label, including the many names of sugar, and meet Wilbur Atwater, who showed that a living body keeps the same energy accounts as a fire.
summary.art: A groundnut on a hairpin burning with a small flame under a steel tumbler of water, with a thermometer standing in the tumbler and a packet of groundnuts with its nutrition table beside it.

intro.hook: A groundnut burns like a tiny candle, but a grain of rice does not. What does a groundnut have inside that a grain of rice has much less of?
intro.text: The food on your plate is fuel for your body, the way wood is fuel for a stove. Scientists measure that fuel in kilocalories. In this unit you burn real foods under a tumbler of water and measure the heat they give out. You cook rice and weigh it before and after. Then you read the label on a packet, and find out what its numbers say and what they leave out.
intro.art: Two small heaps side by side on a steel plate, a few groundnuts and a spoonful of raw rice, with a lit match held above the groundnuts.

outcomes: I can sort foods by their main job, which is giving energy, building the body or protecting it, and explain why one food can do more than one job.
I can explain that a kilocalorie measures the heat in food, and that fat holds about twice the energy of starch or protein in the same weight.
I can run a fair test that burns a food under a tumbler of water, measure the heat, and say how much heat was lost.
I can read a food label: energy per 100 grams and per serving, the order of the ingredients, the names of sugar, and the green or brown dot.
I can explain why the water in cooked food lowers its energy per 100 grams.
I can name protective foods and say what vitamins, minerals and fibre do for the body.
I can explain how the body releases the energy in food, and why the number on a label is only an estimate.
I can describe how scientists showed that a living body follows the same energy rules as a fire.

terms.meaning: A unit for measuring energy. One kilocalorie is the heat that warms one litre of water by one degree Celsius. On a label it is written kcal, and people often call it a calorie.
terms.example: A groundnut kernel holds about 3 kilocalories.
terms.art: A litre bottle of water with a thermometer showing the water one degree warmer after one kilocalorie of heat goes in.

terms.meaning: Another unit of energy that scientists use. One kilocalorie is about 4.2 kilojoules.
terms.example: A packet from another country may show 2,400 kilojoules where an Indian packet shows 570 kilocalories.
terms.art: Two rulers side by side, one marked in inches and one in centimetres, with the same length measured on both.

terms.meaning: A food that mostly gives the body fuel. Foods rich in carbohydrates or fats are energy-giving foods.
terms.example: Rice, roti, potato, ghee and oil.
terms.art: A steel plate with rice, a roti and a spoon of ghee, with small flames drawn above them.

terms.meaning: A food that mostly gives the body protein to build and mend muscles, skin and blood. The body can also burn protein for fuel when it needs to.
terms.example: Dal, egg, paneer, fish and curd.
terms.art: A bowl of dal, an egg and a block of paneer, with a drawing of a muscle beside them.

terms.meaning: A food rich in vitamins and minerals, which help the body fight illness and work properly.
terms.example: Guava, amla, spinach, carrot and papaya.
terms.art: A basket of orange, red and green fruit and vegetables with a small shield drawn above it.

terms.meaning: How much energy a food holds in each 100 grams. Foods with little water and a lot of fat have a high energy density.
terms.example: Ghee has an energy density of about 900 kilocalories in 100 grams. Cucumber has about 15.
terms.art: A balance scale with a small heap of groundnuts on one side and a big heap of cucumber slices on the other, level.

terms.meaning: The amount of food that the maker of a packet counts as one helping. It can be much smaller than what people really eat.
terms.example: A packet of chips may list 30 grams as one serving, and the whole packet may hold four servings.
terms.art: A packet of chips beside a small heap marked 30 grams and a much bigger handful in a bowl.

terms.meaning: The list of everything a packet food is made of. The ingredients are listed from the largest amount by weight to the smallest.
terms.example: If sugar is the first word, there is more sugar than anything else.
terms.art: A packet with its back turned to us and a magnifying glass over the first three words of the ingredient list.

terms.meaning: Sugar that a maker puts into a food. It is different from the sugar that is part of a fruit or milk.
terms.example: The sugar stirred into packaged fruit juice.
terms.art: A glass of juice with a row of sugar spoons lined up beside it.

terms.meaning: The part of salt that matters for health. Too much sodium over many years can harm the heart and kidneys. Salt is about two and a half times the weight of its sodium.
terms.example: A packet of instant noodles can hold more than half a day's salt in one serving.
terms.art: A salt shaker with a small scale showing salt and sodium weighed side by side.

terms.meaning: A food that has had a vitamin or mineral added to it on purpose. Packets show a small +F sign.
terms.example: Iodised salt and fortified atta or oil.
terms.art: A packet of atta with a +F sign and tiny drops going into a stream of flour.

terms.meaning: The part of plant foods that the body cannot digest. It keeps the gut moving and feeds the helpful bacteria that live there.
terms.example: Whole wheat, ragi, vegetables and fruit with their skins.
terms.art: A cross-section of the gut with tiny bacteria feeding on strands of fibre.

terms.meaning: The way every cell in a living body uses oxygen to release the energy stored in food. It is not the same as breathing, but breathing brings the oxygen.
terms.example: When you run, your cells use food faster and you breathe faster to bring more oxygen.
terms.art: A single cell with food and oxygen going in, and heat, movement and carbon dioxide coming out.

terms.meaning: A device that measures the heat that something gives out when it burns or works.
terms.example: Your tumbler of water and thermometer make a simple calorimeter.
terms.art: A burning nut under a tumbler of water with a thermometer, labelled as a simple calorimeter.

terms.meaning: A label column that gives the numbers for the same weight of every food, so you can compare one food with another fairly.
terms.example: Comparing biscuits and murmura per 100 grams shows which one holds more energy in the same weight.
terms.art: Two packets on a scale, each with exactly 100 grams of food poured out beside it.

explanations.concept: Energy in food, and how a kilocalorie is measured
explanations.definition: A kilocalorie is the heat needed to warm one litre of water by one degree Celsius. We measure the energy in food by how much heat it gives out when it burns.
explanations.description: Food is fuel. When a food burns, it joins with oxygen and gives out its stored energy as heat. If that heat warms water, a thermometer tells us how much energy there was. One kilocalorie warms one litre of water by one degree, so two kilocalories warm it by two degrees. A tumbler of 50 millilitres is one twentieth of a litre. So one kilocalorie would warm it by 20 degrees. A groundnut kernel holds about 3 kilocalories, but a home flame wastes most of the heat into the air, so the water gains only part of it. That is why scientists use a closed, insulated metal chamber called a bomb calorimeter. Your body does not burn food in a flame, but the energy released is the same.
examples: A packet that says 570 kilocalories per 100 grams holds enough heat to warm 570 litres of water by one degree.
One whole groundnut kernel weighs about half a gram and holds about 3 kilocalories, enough to warm 50 millilitres of water by up to 60 degrees if none of the heat were lost.
Indian packets show kilocalories. Packets from some other countries show kilojoules, and one kilocalorie is about 4.2 kilojoules.
explanations.art: A groundnut flame under a tumbler of water, with arrows showing some heat going into the water and most heat escaping into the air.

explanations.concept: Three jobs: energy-giving, body-building and protective
explanations.definition: Food does three main jobs. It gives energy, it gives the materials to build and mend the body, and it gives the vitamins and minerals that protect the body and keep it working.
explanations.description: Many schoolbooks sort foods into energy-giving foods, body-building foods and protective foods. Rice, roti and ghee are energy-giving foods. Dal, egg and paneer are body-building foods. Fruit, vegetables and leafy greens are protective foods. The sorting is useful for planning a meal, because a meal with all three jobs covered has what the body needs. But a job is something food does, not a label stuck on the food. A groundnut is called a body-building food, because a quarter of it is protein, yet it burned and heated your water. Your body also burns protein for fuel when it has little else. Curd, milk and eggs do all three jobs at once. So the three groups tell you what a food mostly does in a normal meal. The body decides what it really does.
examples: Dal is called a body-building food. About a fifth of dry dal is protein, and more than half is starch, which is fuel.
Milk gives energy in its fat and milk sugar, building material in its protein and calcium, and protection in its vitamins.
A mango is called a protective food for its vitamins A and C, and it also gives plenty of energy as sugar.
explanations.art: Three circles overlapping like a Venn diagram, labelled energy, building and protection, with groundnuts, milk and rice placed where the circles meet.

explanations.concept: Carbohydrates and fats: the fuel foods, and why fat holds more
explanations.definition: Carbohydrates and fats are the body's main fuels. Carbohydrates give about 4 kilocalories in each gram. Fat gives about 9 kilocalories in each gram.
explanations.description: Starch and sugar are carbohydrates, and they are the body's quick fuel. Your body breaks starch into sugar, and your cells burn the sugar. Fat is a slower, longer-lasting fuel. A gram of fat holds a little more than twice the energy of a gram of starch, because fat has more hydrogen atoms for oxygen to burn. This is why a groundnut, which is nearly half fat, burns well, and rice, which is almost all starch with very little fat, burns poorly in a flame. It is also why ghee holds about 900 kilocalories in 100 grams. Fat is how the body stores energy for later. An animal that has to go a long time without food, such as a camel or a migrating bird, stores fat for the same reason.
examples: 100 grams of sugar holds about 400 kilocalories. 100 grams of ghee holds about 900.
A groundnut is about 45 percent fat. Puffed rice is under 1 percent fat. This is why the groundnut burns for a minute and puffed rice flares and is gone.
Migrating birds store fat before a long flight because a gram of fat holds more energy than a gram of anything else they can carry.
explanations.art: Two bars side by side, one for 100 grams of rice at 350 kilocalories and one for 100 grams of ghee at 900, with the gram weights drawn as equal heaps.

explanations.concept: Protein: building first, fuel when needed
explanations.definition: Proteins are long chains made of small building blocks called amino acids. The body builds its muscles, skin, hair, blood and many other parts from protein.
explanations.description: When you eat protein, your gut breaks it into single amino acids. Your body then joins them again, in a new order, into the proteins it needs. Your body can make some amino acids itself, but there are nine it cannot make, so they must come from food. Different foods carry different amounts of each. Grains such as rice are low in one amino acid called lysine. Pulses such as dal are low in another called methionine. Together, they supply all nine well. Proteins are also a fuel. If a body has too little carbohydrate and fat, it burns protein, at about 4 kilocalories in a gram. Children need protein every day, because they are growing. Adults need it to mend their bodies.
examples: Rice with dal, idli with sambar and roti with rajma each join a grain and a pulse, and are old traditional pairings.
A growing child needs more protein for each kilogram of body weight than an adult does.
Protein from the egg white you eat is taken apart and rebuilt as the muscle in your leg.
explanations.art: A chain of coloured beads for a protein, with a bowl of rice supplying red beads and a bowl of dal supplying blue beads.

explanations.concept: Protective foods: vitamins, minerals and fibre
explanations.definition: Vitamins and minerals are nutrients needed in small amounts, and fibre is the part of plants we cannot digest. Foods rich in them protect the body.
explanations.description: Vitamins and minerals give no energy, but the body cannot work without them. Vitamin A, from carrots, papaya, drumstick leaves and spinach, protects the eyes and the skin. Vitamin C, from amla, guava and lemon, helps the body heal and helps it take in iron. Iron, from ragi, jaggery, dates and leafy greens, helps the blood carry oxygen. Calcium, from milk, curd and ragi, builds bones and teeth. Iodine in iodised salt protects against goitre. Skin makes vitamin D when sunlight falls on it. Vitamin B12 is made by microbes, so plant foods rarely hold any, and vegetarians get it from milk, curd and eggs, or from a supplement a doctor suggests. Tea drunk with a meal holds on to iron and lowers how much the body takes in. A squeeze of lemon on dal or spinach raises it. Fibre keeps the gut moving and feeds helpful gut bacteria.
examples: Amla holds several times more vitamin C than an orange does, weight for weight.
Kamala Sohonie, who in 1939 became the first Indian woman to earn a doctorate in science, later studied neera, the fresh sweet sap of the palm, and found it rich in vitamins.
Ragi holds about 340 milligrams of calcium in 100 grams, and the same weight of milk holds about 120.
explanations.art: A row of fruit, vegetables and ragi, each with a small label showing the vitamin or mineral it gives, in a bright rainbow arc.

explanations.concept: How your body burns food: respiration
explanations.definition: Respiration is the way every living cell uses oxygen to release the energy stored in food.
explanations.description: A flame burns a nut fast, in one step, and nearly all the energy comes out as heat and light. A cell releases the same energy from sugar in many small steps, using oxygen. Each step is run by a different molecule that works like a tiny machine. Some of the energy is caught in a small molecule called ATP, which works like a charged battery that the cell uses to move, build and send signals. The rest warms the body, which is why you are warm. The waste products are carbon dioxide, which you breathe out, and water. Because cells in a flame and cells in a body both start with sugar and oxygen and end with carbon dioxide and water, the total energy released is the same. A hot flame would kill a cell, so the slow steps matter. A body cannot burn food all at once without cooking itself.
examples: When you run, your cells burn sugar faster, so you breathe faster to bring oxygen and you feel warm.
Even asleep, your body uses energy for the heart, breathing, the brain and keeping warm. The brain alone uses about a fifth of an adult's energy, and a larger share of a child's.
Yeast in dough get energy from sugar without oxygen, by fermenting it. They get less energy from the same sugar and make gas and alcohol instead.
explanations.art: A flame on the left and a cell on the right, both with sugar and oxygen going in and carbon dioxide, water and heat coming out, the cell drawn with many small steps.

explanations.concept: Water in food: why energy is counted per 100 grams
explanations.definition: Water holds no energy for the body. The more water a food holds, the less energy it holds in each 100 grams.
explanations.description: Water is part of the weight of nearly every food, but the body cannot get energy from it. Cucumber is about 95 percent water, so 100 grams hold only about 15 kilocalories. Dry foods such as groundnuts, rice and flour have almost no water, so they hold much more in the same weight. When you cook rice, it soaks up two or three times its own weight of water. Nothing is added to the energy, but it is spread over a much heavier pot of food. So 100 grams of cooked rice holds only about a third of the energy of 100 grams of raw rice, and the same pan of rice still gives the same total. Some labels, on ready mixes for example, give one column for the food as sold and another for the food as prepared.
examples: Raw rice holds about 350 kilocalories in 100 grams. Cooked rice holds about 130.
A boiled egg and about 13 grams of groundnuts both hold about 75 kilocalories, but the egg weighs four times as much because of its water.
A hiker who carries dry food, such as chikki and groundnuts, carries much more energy in the same pack than one who carries idli.
explanations.art: A small scoop of raw rice beside a big pot of cooked rice, both labelled with the same total energy.

explanations.definition: A food label is a table and a list on a packet, set by law in India by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India, that says what is in the food and how much.
explanations.description: Start at the nutrition table. Look for the column per 100 grams, because it lets you compare one packet with another fairly. A second column, per serving, shows what the maker counts as one helping. Check how many servings there are in the pack. Then look at the lines: energy in kilocalories, protein, carbohydrate with the sugars inside it, fat, and sodium. Next read the ingredient list. Ingredients are listed from the most by weight to the least, so the first three tell you most of the story. A green dot in a square means vegetarian, and a brown dot means it holds egg, meat or fish. A +F sign means vitamins or minerals have been added. The date tells you when the food should be used by. Percentages on a label are usually worked out for an adult who needs about 2,000 kilocalories a day, so they can mislead for a child.
examples: A biscuit packet shows 480 kilocalories per 100 grams, but only 120 per serving, because a serving is 25 grams.
If the first ingredient on a 'fruit' biscuit is sugar, the biscuit holds more sugar than fruit.
'Sodium' is not salt. To find the salt, multiply the sodium by about two and a half.
explanations.art: The back of a biscuit packet with arrows pointing to the per 100 gram column, the servings line, the ingredient list, the green dot and the date.

explanations.definition: Sugar is the plain name for sucrose, but food makers use many other names for sweet carbohydrates that the body treats in much the same way.
explanations.description: On an ingredient list, sugar may appear as sugar, jaggery, honey, glucose syrup, fructose, dextrose, maltodextrin, invert sugar, malt extract or fruit juice concentrate. A packet can list several of these separately, so each one is small and none is first on the list, even though together they add up to the biggest share. Four grams of sugar is about one level teaspoon. A small packet drink of 200 millilitres with 22 grams of sugar holds more than five teaspoons. Labels in India show total sugars and, on many packets, added sugars. Sugar is a fuel and not a poison, but sweet foods are easy to eat quickly and in large amounts. Jaggery has a little iron and a few minerals that white sugar lacks, but it is still mostly sugar, and the body handles it much the same way.
examples: Ingredients: wheat flour, sugar, glucose syrup, invert sugar, palm oil. Together, the three sugars could weigh more than the flour. The list cannot tell you, but it tells you to look closer.
A teaspoon of sugar is about 4 grams. A 22 gram drink is 5 and a half teaspoons.
Honey, jaggery and sugar all give about 3 to 4 kilocalories in each gram.
explanations.art: Five teaspoons of sugar lined up in front of a small juice carton, with a list of sugar names on a card beside them.

explanations.concept: Where a label's calorie number comes from, and how exact it is
explanations.description: A food label's energy number is usually not measured by burning the packet. Makers work it out by weighing the protein, fat and carbohydrate in the food, and multiplying each by a standard number, about 4 for protein, 9 for fat and 4 for carbohydrate. These standard numbers were worked out in the 1890s by Wilbur Atwater. They are averages. A real body does not get exactly the same from every food, so the number on a label is a good estimate and not an exact measure.
examples: In a careful study published in 2012, almonds gave volunteers about a quarter fewer calories than the standard numbers predicted.
In 2015, Israeli scientists led by Eran Segal and Eran Elinav watched the blood sugar of about 800 people after the same meals, and found that people reacted very differently to the same food.
Cooking changes how much of a food the body can use. Cooked starch is easier to digest than raw.

perspectives.who: Food scientists who use the standard numbers
perspectives.explanation: The averages are close enough to compare foods fairly, and every packet uses the same system, so comparing labels is fair. Without a standard, no two packets could be compared.

perspectives.who: Researchers who study how bodies differ
perspectives.explanation: Bodies differ in how much of a food they take in. Gut bacteria, how the food was chopped and cooked, and a person's own digestion can all change the answer. The number on a label may be right on average and wrong for you.

explanations.art: A packet with a number 570 on it, and three different people eating the same food, with three slightly different numbers floating over them.

explanations.concept: Is the processing the problem, or the nutrients?
explanations.description: Some foods are made in factories from many ingredients and then sealed in packets. Scientists call the most heavily factory-made group ultra-processed foods. Everyone agrees that many of these foods are high in sugar, salt and fat. The argument is about why they seem to be linked to ill health when eaten in large amounts. In a well-known test in 2019, the American scientist Kevin Hall housed 20 adults for four weeks in a hospital ward. For two weeks they ate mostly ultra-processed foods and for two weeks mostly unprocessed foods, in meals matched for sugar, fat, fibre and protein. On the ultra-processed diet, people ate about 500 kilocalories more a day and put on weight. Nobody yet knows exactly why.
examples: Iodised salt, fortified atta, pasteurised milk and frozen peas are all processed, and all of them protect health.
In the 2019 test, people ate faster on the ultra-processed diet. Whether speed is the cause is still unknown.
A packet of puffed snack and a bowl of boiled groundnuts can hold similar energy, but most people eat far more of the snack before they feel full.

perspectives.who: Carlos Monteiro and the team who made the NOVA groups
perspectives.explanation: How much a food has been changed in a factory matters on its own. These foods are made to be soft, sweet and easy to eat quickly, so people eat more of them.
Processing is not one thing. What matters is the amount of sugar, salt, fat and fibre in a food, and a fair rule should look at those, as well as at how a food was made.

explanations.art: Two plates with the same energy: a plate of boiled groundnuts and fruit, and a plate of packet snacks, with two children eating at different speeds.

explanations.concept: How much energy does a child need?
explanations.definition: The energy a body needs depends on its size, its age and how much it moves. A child of 6 to 10 years usually needs about 1,700 to 2,000 kilocalories a day.
explanations.description: Even sitting still, your body uses energy to keep your heart beating, your lungs breathing, your brain thinking and your body warm. This resting energy is the biggest part of what you need. On top of it comes growing, and moving. A child who runs and plays all day needs more than a child who sits. If you eat more energy than you use, your body stores the extra, mostly as fat. If you eat less than you use, your body burns what it has stored. Both can be unhealthy if they go on for a long time. A child who goes hungry for years may grow more slowly. Needs also vary from child to child, so these numbers are a middle, not a rule for every body.
examples: A dancer in training and a child who sits all day may need very different amounts.
A growing child needs a lot of energy for their size, because they are also building a bigger body.
A packet that says 'based on a 2,000 kilocalorie diet' uses an adult number, so a child's share of each nutrient is usually different.
explanations.art: Two children, one running and one reading, each with a small bar showing different energy needs for the same day.

agreed.text: The energy in food can be measured as heat, in kilocalories.
agreed.evidence: When a food burns inside a closed, insulated chamber, the heat it gives out warms a known amount of water. Scientists have done this for well over a hundred years, and the numbers repeat.

agreed.text: Fat holds about 9 kilocalories in each gram, and carbohydrate and protein hold about 4.
agreed.evidence: These averages were worked out by Wilbur Atwater in the 1890s, from burning foods and measuring how much of each food people actually absorbed. Every food label in the world still uses them.

agreed.text: A living body follows the same energy rules as a fire. Energy is changed from one form to another, and none is made or lost.
agreed.evidence: Atwater and his team measured everything that went into a sealed room with a volunteer in it, and everything that came out as heat and work. The two matched very closely.

agreed.text: Almost all the energy in our food was first caught from sunlight by green plants.
agreed.evidence: Plants kept in the dark stop making food and use up what they stored. A few living beings near deep-sea vents use chemical energy instead, but they feed only a very small part of life on Earth.

agreed.text: A body that lacks a vitamin or mineral for a long time can fall ill in a particular way.
agreed.evidence: Goitre fell sharply in places after salt had iodine added to it. Night blindness is linked to too little vitamin A, and anaemia is linked to too little iron.

agreed.text: On a food label, the ingredients are listed from the largest amount by weight to the smallest.
agreed.evidence: This is the rule for packaged food in India, set by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India, and in most other countries.

challenging.claim: Jaggery is a healthy replacement for sugar.
challenging.for: Jaggery is less refined than white sugar and carries a little iron and a few other minerals.
challenging.against: Jaggery is about 95 percent sugar, and the body handles it much as it handles white sugar. The extra minerals are small, so a child would need to eat a large amount to get much of them.

challenging.claim: A calorie is a calorie. All that matters is how many you eat.
challenging.who: Some diet advice and many weight-loss apps.
challenging.for: Energy is never made or lost, so the total energy in and out has to balance.
challenging.against: Bodies take in different amounts from the same food, and foods differ in how filling they are and how fast they are eaten. The balance of energy is true, but the number on a label is an estimate of what a body will take in.

challenging.claim: Protein is the only food that builds muscle, so more protein is always better.
challenging.who: Advertisements for protein powders and bars.
challenging.for: Muscles are mostly protein, and a growing child needs it every day.
challenging.against: The body uses what it needs and burns or stores the rest. A child eating dal, curd, milk, eggs or fish gets enough for building. Exercise and enough energy from other foods matter just as much.

challenging.claim: If the front of a packet says 'multigrain', 'natural', 'low fat' or 'no added sugar', the food is healthy.
challenging.for: Some of these words describe a real difference, such as less fat.
challenging.against: These words are chosen to sell the packet, and they do not tell you the amount of sugar, salt or fat. The nutrition table and the ingredient list at the back give the real numbers.

challenging.claim: You must eat rice and dal in the same meal, or the protein is wasted.
challenging.who: A popular book, Diet for a Small Planet, in 1971.
challenging.for: Rice is low in the amino acid lysine and dal is low in methionine, so together they fit each other well.
challenging.against: The author, Frances Moore Lappé, later wrote that this was stricter than needed. The body keeps a store of amino acids across the day, so a grain and a pulse eaten at different meals still work together.

big_questions.q: A flame and a cell both burn sugar with oxygen and make the same heat. Why does a flame destroy a nut in a minute while your body takes hours?
big_questions.hint: Think of a firework and a slowly burning lamp. What would happen to a cell that got all its energy at once?

big_questions.q: A label gives one calorie number for a food. Is the number a fact about the food, or a fact about the food meeting a body?
big_questions.hint: Remember that different bodies took different amounts from the same almonds, and that cooking changes what a body can take in. Where does the number live?

big_questions.q: If the body can burn protein and store sugar as fat, what does it mean to call a food body-building or energy-giving?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the groundnut did in your tumbler, and what your body does with a day of dal.

big_questions.q: The world grows enough food energy for everyone, according to the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization, yet many people are hungry. How can both be true?
big_questions.hint: Think about who grows food, who can pay for it, how it travels, and how much is thrown away. M. S. Swaminathan spent his life on this question.

big_questions.q: A label counts kilocalories, grams and percentages. What does a label leave out that still matters about a meal?
big_questions.hint: Think of who grew the food, how far it travelled, how it tastes, and who you ate it with.

big_questions.q: A bird stores fat for a flight over a sea. A camel stores it in a hump. A child stores it too. Why do so many living beings store energy as fat and not as sugar?
big_questions.hint: Compare the energy in a gram of fat with a gram of sugar, and think about what carrying the extra weight costs.

big_questions.q: Almost every calorie in your food began as sunlight. When you run, whose energy are you spending?
big_questions.hint: Follow the energy back through the groundnut, the plant, the Sun, and ask where you begin and the meal ends.

story.title: The Heart on the Biscuit Packet
story.note: A made-up story. The science in it is real. Ingredient lists run from the largest amount to the smallest, sugar has many names, and a serving can be far smaller than what a person eats.
text: Every evening at five, Ammamma sat on the veranda in Thrissur with her tea and her biscuits. Nandini sat beside her with a glass of milk. They watched the crows argue on the compound wall.

That month, the doctor told Ammamma that her blood held too much sugar. 'Eat less sweet food,' he said. 'And read what you buy.' Ammamma was seventy-one. Her eyes were tired, and the print on packets had turned into a grey blur.

On Saturday she walked with Nandini to Sebastian Chettan's shop at the corner. Nandini was nine and she held the cloth bag. The shelves were full of bright packets. Sebastian Chettan was a big man with a pencil behind his ear, and he knew every packet in his shop.

'For the sugar, you want these,' he said. He lifted down a green packet with a big heart on the front. In gold letters it said, Multigrain. No Maida. Heart Friendly. 'Our best seller for people like you, Ammamma. Only forty-eight calories a biscuit.'
Ammamma reached for her purse.
'Wait,' said Nandini.
That week at school, her teacher Anitha Miss had given every child a packet from home. 'The front of a packet is an advertisement,' she had said. 'The back is where the facts are. Read the back.'
Nandini turned the packet over. The print was tiny, even for her. She stepped to the door and held it in the light.
'Read it to me,' said Ammamma.

'Ingredients,' Nandini read slowly. 'Whole wheat flour. Sugar. Oats. Glucose syrup. Palm oil. Invert sugar syrup. Salt.' She stopped. 'Ammamma, it says multigrain. But the oats are only third. And there is sugar in it three times.'
'Three times?' Sebastian Chettan frowned.

'Sugar, glucose syrup and invert sugar syrup. They have different names, but they are all sweet. Anitha Miss says the list goes from the most to the least. So the flour is first and sugar is second. But if you put the three sugars together, they might be the biggest part of all.'
Sebastian Chettan took the packet and read the back himself, moving his lips. 'Thirty years,' he said quietly, 'and nobody ever told me to turn it over.'

'There is a table too,' said Nandini. 'The front says forty-eight calories. But that is per biscuit, and one biscuit is ten grams. Here, the table says per one hundred grams. It says four hundred and eighty kilocalories, and twenty-two grams of sugar.'

Ammamma did the sum in her head, the way she had done sums at the market for fifty years. 'Ten biscuits make a hundred grams. Forty-eight times ten is four hundred and eighty. So the table is honest.' She tapped her walking stick on the floor. 'And I eat six every evening.'

'Six biscuits is sixty grams,' said Nandini. 'Twenty-two grams of sugar in a hundred grams. So sixty grams has about thirteen grams of sugar.' She asked Sebastian Chettan for the spoon from his tea counter. 'A level spoon of sugar is about four grams. So that is three spoons, Ammamma. Every evening.'
Nobody said anything. A crow landed on the shop's tin roof and the sound rang through the shop.
Ammamma laughed first. It was a short, surprised laugh. 'I used to read you the newspaper,' she said. 'Now you read me the biscuit.'

She did not throw the biscuits away, and Nandini did not ask her to. They bought a small packet of roasted chana from the next shelf. Nandini read its back too. It said roasted chana, salt, and nothing else. Ammamma would have two biscuits with her tea, and a handful of chana, which would keep her stomach full for longer.
As they were leaving, Sebastian Chettan called after them. 'Nandini, if you come on Mondays, will you read me the back of five more packets? I will give you a peppermint for each.'
On Monday, Nandini found a small card beside the green heart, written in pencil. It said, Read the back first. The first three words tell you the most.

That evening on the veranda, Ammamma drank her tea slowly, with two biscuits and a handful of chana, while the crows argued over the wall. Nandini counted the sugar in her head. Some things, she thought, are written in very small print, and they matter the most.
story.epiphany: The big words were on the front of the packet. The facts were at the back, in the order of weight.
ask: Why does it help that an ingredient list goes from the most to the least?
If three kinds of sugar are listed separately, how could you find out how much sugar there is altogether?
Why might a maker choose a small serving size for the front of a packet?
